lr-flaw-honors-scholarship-conditional: Two defensible answers. The inference actually runs through the probation premise: 'never on probation' is a necessary condition for completing honors, and the argument treats it as sufficient (A). But the conclusion is also the straight converse of premise 1 (scholarship recipients -> honors), which B describes. A is the more precise description of the inferential step the argument makes; B describes the shape of the conclusion. Recommend tightening so only one choice names the operative flaw (e.g., drop or rewrite B).
lr-flaw-deficit-two-options: Two defensible answers. The 'must either cut spending or raise taxes' claim is stated as a premise, so on strict LSAT convention B (false dilemma) is less attackable than D, which names an unaddressed gap (cuts might also deepen the slowdown). Chose D, but many strong test-takers will pick B. Consider rewording the premise or B so the dilemma is unmistakably given rather than assumed.
lr-flaw-painting-value-senses: E (equivocation on 'value': aesthetic vs. monetary/historical) is the intended structural flaw and the best answer, but C (viewers' knowledge that a work is a reproduction diminishes the experience) is a genuine and fairly direct objection to the key premise. C is attackable as 'disputing a premise' rather than naming a reasoning flaw, but it is closer than a typical wrong answer.
lr-flaw-sleep-grades-start-times: B (third-variable/correlation-causation) is the best answer, but C (later start times are the only way to get more sleep) is also a real gap in the leap from 'more sleep' to 'later start times.' Acceptable as-is; B is clearly the primary flaw, noting only that C is stronger than an ideal distractor.
lr-resolve-explain-bakery-price-cut: A is the only choice that helps at all, but the arithmetic is not airtight: a 10% cut with 25% more loaves gives ~12.5% more revenue if all loaves are regular; A only resolves this if the cheap small loaves also cannibalized regular-loaf sales. 'Most of the additional loaves' leaves open a reading in which regular-loaf sales held steady and revenue still rises. Consider tightening A (e.g., 'many customers switched from regular loaves to a new small loaf priced at less than half...').
lr-resolve-explain-norland-textile-wages: E is the intended composition-effect answer (low-wage firms closing raises the industry average). B (much more overtime) is arguably defensible under an 'earnings' reading of 'average wage'; the stimulus's 'raised the wages it paid' points to pay rates, which excludes B, but a careful test-taker could see two answers. Consider wording the stimulus as 'average hourly wage' to close this off.
lr-sufficient-assumption-veltrax-trials: E is the answer that closes the gap (no large controlled trials by anyone else). B is a tempting restatement of the premise chain but does not establish that no large trials were run. Clean, but note B reads as a very close paraphrase of the premises, which is slightly unusual as a wrong answer.
lr-psa-application-document-withholding: A is clearly best, but the principle only restricts withholding ('may withhold only if'); it never requires withholding. So choice D (agency releases a document despite safety risk) does not technically violate the principle either. Consider rewording the principle to also require withholding when safety is endangered, or revise D so it is a withholding decision that fails the principle.
lr-main-conclusion-downtown-parking-hous: D is the best answer, but the closing sentence ('Indeed, it is the businesses, far more than the council, that stand to gain') could be read by some test-takers as the main conclusion. C is kept wrong only by the overstatement 'more than anyone else' versus 'far more than the council.' Consider tightening so the final sentence reads unambiguously as support (e.g. 'In fact, ... stand to gain') or soften the wrong-answer trap.
lr-parallel-method-bridge-collapse-cause: A is the best match (three options, two eliminated by evidence, third concluded). B is a tempting near-match but is hedged ('probably') and its elimination evidence is weaker; still defensible as the single answer. No change strictly needed.
